content: Fruits rich in vitamin A include cantaloupe, mango, papaya, and passion fruit. Berries and citrus fruits are also significant sources of vitamin C. Other fruits high in vitamin C, such as guava, kiwi, longan, and lychee, were identified based on a threshold of at least 50 mg of ascorbic acid per 100 grams in their consumable form. Additionally, bananas, avocados, coconuts (flesh), and other high-fat fruits were categorized separately. Other fruits, including apples, peaches, pears, and pineapples, were grouped into a general category. Vitamin A-rich fruits were defined according to the WHO/UNICEF Infant and Young Child Feeding Indicators manual (2021). For vitamin C-rich fruits, the selection was based on their ascorbic acid content. Vegetables were categorized into subgroups based on their characteristics and nutrient profiles. These included medium to dark green leafy vegetables, brassicas (e.g., broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage, Brussels sprouts, kohlrabi), vitamin A-rich orange vegetables (e.g., carrots, squash, pumpkin, orange-fleshed sweet potato), peppers and tomatoes, immature peas and beans (seeds and pods), and other vegetables (e.g., cucumbers, onions, corn, mushrooms, turnips, iceberg lettuce). Brassicas were further grouped by the part of the plant consumed and their color (e.g., white versus green leaves) due to differences in nutrient values. Sweet red peppers were grouped with tomatoes and similar items, rather than with vitamin A-rich orange vegetables. Specific considerations included grouping bean sprouts with vegetables rather than legumes due to their water and protein content. Non-staple root vegetables, such as parsnips, rutabagas, turnips, and salsify, were grouped with other vegetables because of their higher water content compared to staple roots and tubers. Onions, shallots, and leeks were classified as vegetables rather than condiments. Unspecified peas or beans were classified based on their water and macronutrient content, aligning them with either dried legumes or fresh peas and beans in pods. Dairy products were divided into milk, yogurt (including fermented dairy like kefir or buttermilk), and cheese. All forms of yogurt and fermented milk were grouped together due to similarities in water content and consumption quantities. Sweetened yogurt products were included in quantity estimates but matched with unsweetened yogurt for nutrient profile calculations. Products marketed as yogurt drinks with low protein, high water, and high sugar content were excluded. Protein sources were categorized into eggs, legumes/pulses (and flours made from them), soy foods, peanuts/groundnuts, tree nuts, seeds (and their pastes), various meats (beef, lamb, mutton, goat, game meat), pork, poultry, liver, and fish. Fish were further divided into small fish eaten with bones and larger fish not eaten with bones. Liver was separated from other organ meats due to its distinct nutrient profile and higher consumption rates. Seafood (e.g., bivalves, crustaceans, cephalopods) was excluded from modeling due to its rare consumption and disproportionate influence on nutrient profiles. Data sources for dietary modeling inputs were derived from various national and sub-national studies across multiple countries. These datasets informed the development of food item lists, maximum quantities for food subgroups, and allowed consumption frequencies. The data were collected from diverse geographic regions and populations, ensuring representation and reliability. Specific studies and datasets were used to analyze food consumption patterns, nutrient adequacy, and dietary recommendations for infants and young children.
